answer.text:
Yes. With finite-gain inverters the loop is stabilized.

Break the loop and model each inverter at its
switching point as an inverting low-pass,

$$ H_0(s) = \frac{-g_m R_0}{1+sR_0 C_0} $$

$C_0$ is the intrinsic load, $R_0$ the output
resistance, $-g_mR_0=-A_0$ the small signal gain.

Put $C_L$ on one node:

$$ H_L(s) = \frac{-A_0}{1+sR_0(C_0+C_L)} $$

The small signal loop gain of the 3 in a ring is

$$ L(s)=H_L(s)H_0^2(s)=
\frac{(-A_0)^3}{[1+s\tau_L][1+s\tau_0]^2}$$

where $\tau_0=R_0C_0$, $\tau_L=R_0(C_0+C_L)$.

At dc, $L_0=-A_0^3$. This is a negative feedback loop.
It oscillates only if the poles contribute an
extra $180^{\circ}$ lag at a frequency where
$|L|\ge 1$, i.e. Barkhausen $L(j\omega)=1$.

Let

$$\phi_L = \tan^{-1}\omega\tau_L,\qquad
  \phi_0 = \tan^{-1}\omega\tau_0 .$$

$$ \angle H_L = 180^{\circ}-\phi_L,\;
   \angle H_0 = 180^{\circ}-\phi_0 $$

$$\angle L = 3\cdot 180^{\circ}-\phi_L-2\phi_0 .$$

Mod $360^{\circ}$, $\angle L=0$ requires

$$\phi_L+2\phi_0 = 180^{\circ} \tag{1}$$
$$\tan^{-1}\omega\tau_L+2\tan^{-1}\omega\tau_0=\pi .$$

The magnitude is

$$|L| = \frac{A_0^3}
{\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau_L)^2}\,[1+(\omega\tau_0)^2]} .
\tag{2}$$

For identical stages $\tau_L=\tau_0$ this gives
$\tan^{-1}\omega\tau_0=60^{\circ}$, $\omega\tau_0=\sqrt3$,
$|L|=A_0^3/8$. $A_0>2$ oscillates.

Now let $C_L\to\infty$, $\tau_L\gg\tau_0$.
From (1), $\phi_L\approx 90^{\circ}$ for any
reasonable $\omega\gg 1/\tau_L$, so we need

$$2\phi_0\approx 90^{\circ},\quad \phi_0\approx 45^{\circ},$$

i.e.

$$\omega_{180}\approx \frac1{\tau_0} .$$

The $180^{\circ}$ frequency stays finite, determined
by the fast inverters. At that frequency from (2)

$$|L|\approx \frac{A_0^3}{(\omega_{180}\tau_L)\cdot 2}
 = \frac{A_0^3}{2\,\tau_L/\tau_0}\to 0
 \;\;{\rm as}\;\; \tau_L\to\infty .$$

In fact $C_L\to\infty$ is an ac short to ground.
The loop gain goes to zero at any finite frequency.
Phase $180^{\circ}$ is reached only where there is
no gain. Routh-Hurwitz on

$$(1+s\tau_L)(1+s\tau_0)^2+A_0^3=0$$

gives stability for

$$\frac{\tau_L}{\tau_0} > \frac{1+A_0^3}{2} .$$

So the linear equilibrium, all inverters biased
at $V_{th}$, becomes stable.

Physically, $V_1$ becomes very slow, $V_2,V_3$
follow quasi-statically. The two fast inverters
in cascade are a non-inverting high gain $+A_2A_3$.
Then

$$C_L \frac{dV_1}{dt} = I_1(V_3)=I_1(g(V_1))$$

with $dg/dV_1>0$, $dI_1/dV_3=-g_{m1}<0$.
This is first-order negative feedback:

$$\frac{d}{dV_1}\frac{dV_1}{dt}<0.$$

$V_1$ approaches the $I_{p}=I_{n}$ equilibrium
asymptotically, with no overshoot. Overshoot,
which requires the delay of inv2-inv3 to be
comparable to the $R_0C_L$ time, is what sustains
the normal ring limit cycle. For $C_L\to\infty$
the swing needed to switch inv2, $\sim I\,t_d/C_L$,
goes to zero. The circuit settles to a dc analog
value, not rail to rail.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly explains that a very large capacitor on one node creates a dominant pole, driving loop gain below unity at the required phase condition. The resulting slow-node, quasi-static settling explanation also agrees with the golden solution.

answer.text:
Yes. With one stage heavily loaded the loop
becomes a stable negative feedback loop.

Model the inverter in the linear region around
its switching threshold by

$$ A(s) = \frac{-A_0}{1+s\tau}$$

$A_0 = g_mR_{out} >0$, $\tau = R_{out}C$.
Let $\tau_0$ be the intrinsic delay of the unloaded
inverter and $\tau_1$ the delay of the loaded
inverter,

$$p_0 = \frac1{\tau_0}\,,\quad p_1=\frac1{\tau_1}
 =\frac{1}{R_{out}(C_0+C_L)} .$$

Breaking the loop, the small signal loop gain is

$$ L(s) = \left(\frac{-A_0}{1+s/p_1}\right)
         \left(\frac{-A_0}{1+s/p_0}\right)^2
       = \frac{-A_0^{3}}{(1+s/p_1)(1+s/p_0)^2} .$$

At DC $L=-A_0^3$, i.e. $180^{\circ}$.
Oscillation start-up needs

$$L(j\omega)=1$$

i.e. $180^{\circ}$ more phase lag from the
three poles,

$$\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega}{p_1}+2\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega}{p_0}=\pi \tag{1}$$

with

$$|L|=\frac{A_0^3}{\sqrt{1+(\omega/p_1)^2}\,
 \left[1+(\omega/p_0)^2\right]}\ge 1 .\tag{2}$$

(1) always has a solution $\omega_{180}$, since
the left side goes monotonically from 0 to $3\pi/2$.

Let $C_L\to\infty$, i.e. $p_1\to 0$.
For any finite $\omega>0$,
$\tan^{-1}(\omega/p_1)\to \pi/2$. Then (1) gives

$$\frac{\pi}{2}+2\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega_{180}}{p_0}\to \pi$$

i.e.

$$\omega_{180}\to p_0 .$$

The phase crossover stays finite. But then

$$|L(j\omega_{180})|\approx 
\frac{A_0^3}{(\omega_{180}/p_1)\cdot 2}\to 0$$

because $p_1\to 0$. In particular for large enough
$C_L$, $|L|<1$ at the $180^{\circ}$ frequency.
The Barkhausen condition fails.

In Routh-Hurwitz terms, $1-L(s)=0$ is

$$(1+s\tau_1)(1+s\tau_0)^2+A_0^3=0$$

i.e.

$$s^3+a_2s^2+a_1s+a_0=0$$

with $a_2=p_1+2p_0$, $a_1=2p_1p_0+p_0^2$,
$a_0=(1+A_0^3)p_1p_0^2$. Stability needs
$a_2a_1>a_0$, i.e.

$$2p_1^2+(4-A_0^3)p_0p_1+2p_0^2>0.$$

For $p_1=p_0$ and $A_0^3\gg 8$ this is $<0$:
unstable bias point, oscillation starts.
For $p_1\to 0$ this is $>0$: the bias point
becomes stable.

Physically, make $C_L$ dominant. The $C_L$ node
$V_1$ is slow, the other two inverters are
essentially instantaneous. Put $V_{in1}=h(V_1)$
where $h=f\circ f$ is the double inversion,
non-inverting, high gain around the threshold.
Then to first order

$$C_L\frac{dV_1}{dt}=I_P(V_{in1},V_1)-I_N(V_{in1},V_1)
\equiv I(V_1).$$

$I(V_1)>0$ for $V_1$ low, $<0$ for $V_1$ high,
strictly decreasing. There is one zero,
$V_1\approx V_{th}$, and

$$\frac{dV_1}{dt}$$

always pushes $V_1$ toward it. There is no overshoot.

In time domain: as soon as $V_1$ crosses $V_{th}$,
the fast inverters immediately flip the input of
the first inverter and reverse its output current,
before $V_1$ can swing to the rail. $V_1$ is
trapped at the analog threshold. The odd ring
has no digital stable state, but it has an analog
stable state with all inverters linear, i.e.
essentially single-dominant-pole negative
feedback.

answer.text:
Yes. In the ideal gate--delay model the period would simply
grow $\propto C_L$, but that model breaks down when the edge
at the $C_L$ node becomes much slower than the other delays.

Label the $C_L$ node $x$, and the other two nodes $y,z$.
For $C_L$ very large, $x$ moves on a time scale
$\sim R_{out}C_L$ much longer than the propagation time of the
other inverters. Hence, on the time scale of $x$, the other
inverters simply follow their static voltage transfer
characteristic $f(\cdot)$, which is decreasing, saturates at
the rails, and crosses $V_{in}=V_{out}$ at $V_M\approx V_{DD}/2$:

$$
y=f(x),\qquad z=f(y),\qquad 
\text{drive to }x = f(z)=f\!\bigl(f\!\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\bigr)\equiv F(x).
$$

The dynamics of the only slow node are first order,

$$
C_L\frac{dx}{dt}\;\propto\;F(x)-x .
$$

$F$ is again a decreasing inverter-like characteristic, with
a unique intersection with $F(x)=x$ at $x=V_M$. If $x<V_M$,
then $F(x)>x$ and the first inverter pulls $x$ up; if
$x>V_M$, then $F(x)<x$ and it pulls $x$ down. So $V_M$ is an
attracting fixed point, and a first-order system cannot
sustain a limit cycle. Any transient ringing decays.

In small-signal terms, each inverter is $-A_0/(1+s\tau_i)$,
and the closed-loop poles satisfy

$$
(1+s\tau_L)(1+s\tau_0)^2+A_0^{3}=0 .
$$

By Routh-Hurwitz this becomes stable for
$\tau_L/\tau_0 \gtrsim (1+A_0^{3})/2$, i.e. for sufficiently
large $C_L$. The large capacitor is dominant-pole
compensation for what is, at dc, a three-inversion negative
feedback loop: the excess phase can no longer reach
$180^\circ$ with loop gain $\ge 1$.

Thus for arbitrarily large $C_L$ the ring does not oscillate.
It settles with all three nodes at about the inverter
switching voltage $V_M$, all inverters on in their
high-gain region.

answer.text:
Yes. The naive delay argument, that a larger $C_L$ only makes
the period longer, assumes ideal logic gates. A real inverter is
a finite-gain amplifier with a finite output resistance.

Let $X$ be the node loaded by $C_L$, and let $C_p$ be the
ordinary parasitic capacitance at the other two nodes.
Near its switching voltage $V_M$ an inverter can be modelled as

$$ -\,\frac{A_0}{1+s/\omega_p}\qquad 
\omega_p=\frac1{R_oC_p}$$

for the two unloaded stages, and

$$ -\,\frac{A_0}{1+s/\omega_L}\qquad 
\omega_L=\frac1{R_oC_L}\ll \omega_p$$

for the stage driving $C_L$. $A_0$ is the low frequency
magnitude of the inverter gain.

The three inversions contribute $3\times180^{\circ}$ around
the loop. For oscillation the three $RC$ poles must supply
another $180^{\circ}$ at a frequency at which the loop gain
magnitude is at least unity.

The loaded pole can supply at most $90^{\circ}$. Hence the
other $180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}$ must come from the two fast
poles, requiring a frequency of order $\omega_p$ or higher:
for $\omega<\omega_p$ the total pole lag is
$<90^{\circ}+45^{\circ}+45^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$.

But at $\omega\gtrsim\omega_p$,

* the two fast stages have magnitudes $\lesssim A_0/\sqrt2$ each,
* the loaded stage has magnitude
  $$\frac{A_0}{\sqrt{1+(\omega/\omega_L)^2}}
   \approx A_0\frac{\omega_L}{\omega}
   \lesssim A_0\frac{\omega_L}{\omega_p}
   =A_0\frac{C_p}{C_L}.$$

Thus the loop gain magnitude at any frequency where the
phase condition can be met is at most

$$|L| \;\lesssim\; A_0^{3}\,\frac{C_p}{C_L}\,\frac12 .$$

For $C_L \gtrsim \tfrac12 A_0^{3}C_p$ this is $<1$, and for
still larger $C_L$ it tends to zero. Barkhausen's criterion
can never be satisfied.

In time-domain terms, $X$ then moves so slowly that
inverters 2 and 3 act as an essentially instantaneous
non-inverting buffer from $X$ back to the input of inverter 1.
Inverter 1 therefore has its output fed back to its own
input, a stable connection. The only dc solution,
$V_1=V_2=V_3=V_M$, becomes stable: perturbations decay
instead of growing into a limit cycle. The ring settles
with all inverters biased in their transition region,
drawing static current, and does not oscillate.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that an arbitrarily large capacitor on one node creates a dominant pole, causing sufficient loop-gain roll-off that the Barkhausen condition cannot be met. The phase/gain and time-domain explanations are consistent with the essential result.

answer.text:
Yes. It does not merely oscillate more slowly; beyond a certain
$C_L$ oscillation is quenched altogether.

Linearise the inverters about their switching voltage $V_M$.
Let a stage have (magnitude of) low-frequency gain $A_v=g_mr_o$ and
output resistance $r_o$. Let $C_0$ be the normal node capacitance,
$\tau_0=r_oC_0$, and for the loaded node $\tau_L=r_o(C_L+C_0)\approx
r_oC_L$.

The closed-loop characteristic equation is

$$
\bigl(1+s\tau_L\bigr)\bigl(1+s\tau_0\bigr)^2 + A_v^{\,3}=0,
$$

i.e.

$$
a_3s^3+a_2s^2+a_1s+a_0=0
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_3&=\tau_L\tau_0^2, &
a_2&=\tau_0^2+2\tau_L\tau_0,\\
a_1&=\tau_L+2\tau_0, &
a_0&=1+A_v^3 .
\end{aligned}
$$

By Routh–Hurwitz the $V_M$ equilibrium is stable iff
$a_2a_1>a_3a_0$. But as $\tau_L\to\infty$,

$$
\frac{a_2a_1}{a_3a_0}
\;\approx\;
\frac{(2\tau_L\tau_0)(\tau_L)}{\tau_L\tau_0^2(1+A_v^3)}
= \frac{2\tau_L}{\tau_0(1+A_v^3)}\;\longrightarrow\;\infty .
$$

So for sufficiently large $C_L$ (roughly $\tau_L/\tau_0\gtrsim A_v^3/2$)
all closed-loop poles move into the left half-plane: the metastable
point becomes *stable*.

Physically: with $C_L$ huge, node $B$ moves so slowly that the second
and third inverters follow it quasi-statically and stay in their
high-gain region. The loop then behaves like a single dominant-pole
stage in negative feedback, not like three rail-to-rail logic gates
chasing each other. A small rise of $B$ above $V_M$ is amplified
(non-inverted) through inverters 2 and 3 to the input of inverter 1,
which pulls $B$ back down, and vice versa — with no overshoot, because
the motion of $B$ is essentially first order.

Hence for arbitrarily large $C_L$ the circuit settles to

$$
V_A \approx V_B \approx V_C \approx V_M,
$$

with all inverters biased in their transition region, and does not
oscillate.

answer.text:
The network is nothing more than a three-stage ring oscillator.  
With an odd number of inversions the loop already possesses the required 180° phase shift at dc, so the only other requirement for oscillation is that the magnitude of the loop gain exceed unity at some frequency.  

Placing the extra capacitance CL on one node

1. adds another low-frequency pole to the open-loop transfer function, and  
2. increases the delay through that particular inverter,  

but it does not change the dc (low–frequency) gain of the inverter, which is still very large (|A0| ≫ 1).  
Hence, even when CL is made very large the loop-gain magnitude is still well above one at ω = 0, and there will always be a (lower) frequency at which |Aβ| = 1 while the total phase shift is 180° + 360°k.  

What changes is the oscillation frequency:

fosc ≈ 1 / [2N (tp0 + Δtp)]  with Δtp ≅ Rout·CL

so fosc falls roughly in inverse proportion to CL.  
As CL → ∞ the period (and the start-up time) → ∞, i.e. the oscillator becomes arbitrarily slow, but the small-signal conditions for oscillation are still satisfied.

Practical limit: the circuit will appear “dead” only when CL is so large that the transistors’ finite static currents (or leakage) can no longer move the node past the switching threshold in any reasonable time. For any finite CL that the devices can eventually charge or discharge, the ring will still start and oscillate—just at a proportionally lower frequency.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer reaches the opposite conclusion: sufficiently large one-node loading can make the oscillator fail, rather than merely slow down. It does mention the added pole and delay, but incorrectly assumes high DC loop gain guarantees a frequency satisfying both Barkhausen conditions.

answer.text:
Take the three–inverter ring oscillator in two steps.

1.  What sets the oscillation frequency  
   Each inverter has an effective output resistance R and is driving the
   capacitance that appears at its output.  
   The small-signal (first-order) transfer function of one stage is  

        A(s) = –A0 /(1+s R Ctot)          with   Ctot = Cint + CL

   (A0 is the low-frequency gain, Cint the intrinsic node capacitance and
   CL the external load that we have added).

   •  The – sign supplies the fundamental 180° phase shift of an inverter.  
   •  The pole at ωp = 1/(R Ctot) contributes an additional phase
      –tan-1(ω/ωp).  
   With three identical stages the total phase is

        Φloop(ω) = 3·(–π ­– tan-1(ωRCtot))

   The ring will oscillate at the frequency ω0 for which Φloop = –2π,
   i.e.

        3π + 3 tan-1(ω0 R Ctot) = 2π  →  tan-1(ω0 R Ctot) = π/3
        ⇒  ω0 = (π / 3) · 1/(R Ctot)

   Thus      f0 ≈ 0.17 / (R Ctot)  ∝ 1/CL.

   As CL is made larger the pole moves down, the required –60°/stage is
   obtained at a proportionally lower frequency, so the oscillation
   simply slows down.

2.  Is the start-up gain still high enough?  
   The loop-gain magnitude at ω0 is

        |Aloop(jω0)| = [ A0 / √(1+(ω0 RCtot)²) ]³
                      = [ A0 / √(1+(π/3)²) ]³ ≈ (0.69 A0)³

   A0 (the dc gain of a CMOS inverter) is independent of the external
   capacitive load, so |Aloop| is essentially the same no matter how big
   CL is.  As long as A0 ≳ 2 the cube of 0.69·A0 is well above unity and
   the oscillation starts and grows.

   Only two non-ideal effects can really stop it:

   •  CL → ∞ ⇒ ω0 → 0, the period becomes infinite, so in the limit of an
     infinite capacitance the circuit never changes state – but this is
     a mathematical limit, not a practical one.

   •  A load so large that the static leakage currents of the devices
     equal the charging / discharging current; then the node cannot be
     driven far enough from the switching threshold.  In ordinary CMOS
     logic this would require capacitances many orders of magnitude
     larger than those encountered on a chip.

Conclusion  
For any finite, practical value of CL the ring oscillator will still
oscillate; its frequency merely drops approximately in inverse
proportion to CL.  It “fails” only in the unphysical limit where CL
becomes infinite (or when leakage rather than dynamic current dominates
– again an impractical situation for normal values of CL).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer assumes the added capacitance loads all three stages equally and concludes that any finite load merely slows oscillation. The question’s one-node asymmetry creates a dominant pole that can make the loop fail to oscillate for sufficiently large CL, so the central conclusion is wrong.

answer.text:
A single-ended ring oscillator keeps oscillating as long as two conditions are satisfied  

1. Static loop gain magnitude > 1 and an odd number of inversions (180° phase shift).  
2. Each stage is able to move its output far enough past the switching threshold of the next stage that the latter will in turn switch.

The first condition is completely independent of the load capacitance that happens to be connected to one of the nodes; the dc (low-frequency) gain of a CMOS inverter is set by device transconductance/resistive output and does not change when a capacitor is hung on the output.

The capacitor only adds delay.  
For one stage the small-signal transfer function is approximately  

  Vout(s)/Vin(s) ≈ −A0 /(1 + sτ) ,  τ ≃ Ron · CL

so the pole moves toward the origin as CL grows.  
For an N-stage ring, the oscillation frequency is

  fosc ≈ 1/(2Nτ)

therefore fosc falls roughly in inverse proportion to CL. If CL is made “arbitrarily large”, τ becomes “arbitrarily large” and the frequency tends toward zero, but the Barkhausen phase-condition can still be satisfied, so mathematically the circuit still oscillates – it just does it very, very slowly.

What stops it in practice?

• Finite output current: the edges rise and fall at Iout/CL. If CL is so large that leakage currents (or any dc load) dominate before the node has been charged/discharged past the switching threshold, the stage will never complete the transition and oscillation will die.  
• Limited noise margin: with an enormous CL the transition is so slow that noise can disturb the state or the loop may get trapped in a metastable operating point.  
• Device leakage, charge sharing, and subthreshold conduction eventually balance the small charging currents for very slow edges and prevent rail-to-rail motion.

Hence:

Ideal, small-signal point of view – No, the oscillator does not fail; its frequency merely approaches zero as CL→∞.

Real hardware – Yes, beyond some finite CLmax (set by the maximum drive current of the inverters, leakage, and required noise margin) the ring will fail to start or will stall.

The key mechanism is that the dominant pole on the singly loaded node causes enough loop gain/phase roll-off for oscillation to fail.
